title: Scale-Aware Trident Networks for Object Detection
venue: IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)

problem.summary: Scale variation is a central obstacle for both one- and two-stage detectors: image pyramids handle it but are too slow at inference, while feature pyramids approximate it cheaply by extracting different-scale regions from different backbone levels whose parameters differ, breaking feature consistency across scales.
statements: Object instance scales vary over a wide range, and very small or very large objects particularly impede detectors.
Image-pyramid methods raise inference time, making them less favorable for practical applications.
Feature pyramids (e.g. FPN) extract region features of different scales from different levels generated by different sets of parameters, sacrificing feature consistency across scales.

evidence.quote: However, a central issue for both methods is the handling of scale variation. The scales of object instances could vary in a wide range, which impedes the detectors, especially those very small or very large ones.
Nevertheless, the increase of inference time makes the image pyramid methods less favorable for practical applications.

However, region features of objects with different scales are extracted from different levels of FPN backbone, which in turn are generated with different sets of parameters. This makes feature pyramids an unsatisfactory alternative for image pyramids.

background.summary: The paper builds on image-pyramid and feature-pyramid scale handling (SSD, FPN, PANet, SNIP/SNIPER) and on dilated convolution for receptive-field control; its claimed gap is that no prior work isolates and studies the effect of the receptive field itself on detection across object scales.

relatedWork.name: FPN
relatedWork.relation: prior feature-pyramid scale handling that the paper positions against
relatedWork.quote: FPN [25] (Figure 1(b)) further augments a top-down pathway and lateral connections to incorporate strong semantic information in high-level features.

relatedWork.name: SNIP
relatedWork.relation: prior scale-normalization training scheme with the same motivation
relatedWork.quote: SNIP [38] proposes a scale normalization method to train objects that fall into the desired scale range for each resolution during multi-scale training.

relatedWork.name: Dilated convolution (Yu & Koltun)
relatedWork.relation: mechanism used to vary receptive fields across branches
relatedWork.quote: Dilated convolution [41] (aka Atrous convolution [20]) enlarges the convolution kernel with original weights by performing convolution at sparsely sampled locations, thus increasing the receptive field size without additional cost.

relatedWork.name: Faster R-CNN
relatedWork.quote: Faster R-CNN [35] first proposes a unified end-to-end framework for object detection.

evidence.quote: Nevertheless, as far as we know, there is no previous work that studies the impact of the receptive field in isolation.
The most suitable receptive field is strongly correlated with the scale of objects.

solution.summary: TridentNet replaces blocks in the backbone's last stage with parallel trident branches that share weights but use different dilation rates, producing scale-specific feature maps with uniform representational power; a scale-aware training scheme samples only objects whose sizes fall in each branch's valid range, and a one-branch fast approximation retains most of the gain at baseline cost.
solution.approach: A weight-sharing multi-branch trident block with distinct dilation rates per branch, trained with scale-aware sampling of object sizes and approximated at inference by the middle branch only.
components: trident blocks: parallel residual branches differing only in dilation rate (default 1, 2, 3)
weight sharing across branches and across the RPN/R-CNN heads
scale-aware training with per-branch valid ranges [0, 90], [30, 160], [90, inf]
trident blocks placed in the conv4 stage of ResNet
TridentNet Fast: single middle-branch inference approximation
NMS / soft-NMS to merge detections from the branches during full inference

evidence.quote: We construct a parallel multi-branch architecture in which each branch shares the same transformation parameters but with different receptive fields.
we adopt a scale-aware training scheme to specialize each branch by sampling object instances of proper scales for training.
A trident block consists of multiple parallel branches in which each shares the same structure with the original convolution block except the dilation rate.
Here we propose TridentNet Fast, a fast approximation of TridentNet with only one branch during inference.

experiments.summary: All experiments are on COCO (trainval35k/minival, plus test-dev), starting from a re-implemented Faster R-CNN baseline in MXNet with ResNet-50/101 (optionally deformable), ablating branch count, trident-block stage/number, scale-aware ranges and fast approximation, then comparing against SNIP, SNIPER, Cascade R-CNN, DCNv2, FPN and ASPP.

benchmarks.split: minival, vs FPN/ASPP with 2fc head, ResNet-101

evidence.quote: On the COCO dataset, our TridentNet with ResNet-101 backbone achieves state-of-the-art single-model results of 48.4 mAP.
TridentNet Fast achieves 41.0 AP which improves 1.2 AP over the baseline with no computation cost.
As can be noticed, four branches do not bring further improvement over three branches.

limitations.summary: The full multi-branch network is slow at inference and is approximated by a single branch with a small AP drop; scale-aware training shrinks effective samples per branch and can overfit; the headline 48.4 AP additionally relies on multi-scale image-pyramid testing.
items: Full TridentNet has slow inference speed because of its branching nature; TridentNet Fast trades some accuracy for it.
Scale-aware training reduces effective samples per branch and may cause over-fitting in each branch.
Four branches bring no further improvement over three branches, so scaling the branch count does not help.
The best result (48.4 AP) requires image-pyramid testing on top of multi-scale training, soft-NMS and deformable convolutions.

evidence.quote: A major drawback of TridentNet is the slow inference speed due to its branching nature.

We conjecture that the scaleaware training design prevents each branch from training objects of extreme scales, but may also bring about the over-fitting problem in each branch caused by reduced effective samples.

applications.detail: One of the authors' affiliations is TuSimple, an autonomous-driving company.

deploymentClaims: TridentNet Fast incurs no additional time cost compared with a standard Faster RCNN detector
The authors present the approach as more desirable than image-pyramid methods for practical uses

evidence.quote: This property makes TridentNet more desirable over other methods for practical uses.
In this way, TridentNet Fast incurs no additional time cost compared with a standard Faster RCNN detector.
